European elderberry (S. nigra) cultivars exist and can be grown too, but the American types are hardier and better adapted across most of the country.

seasoned: Fresh elderberries are highly perishable and should not be held at room temperature; process or refrigerate them the day you pick. Remember they are NOT a fresh eating fruit: raw ripe berries are unpleasant and mildly toxic, so plan to cook, juice, or dry them rather than store fresh.

beginner: In the fridge, elderberry clusters keep only a few days, so plan to use them quickly. A handy trick: freeze the clusters for a bit, then the berries pop off the stems easily with a fork. Keep the stems out of whatever you make.

It fruits best on canes that are one to three years old, so each winter cut out the oldest canes at the base (older than about three years) plus anything dead, broken, or crowded, and leave the strong younger stems. If your elderberry has become an overgrown tangle that fruits poorly, you can cut the whole thing to the ground in late winter and it will bounce right back.

Each dormant season remove canes older than about three years at ground level, along with any dead, broken, weak, or crowded stems, keeping the most vigorous younger canes. If a planting has grown into a tangled, unproductive thicket, you can cut the entire clump to the ground in late winter to renew it; it will regrow vigorously and be fruiting again within a year or two.
